questions.subtopic: Joint Ventures: Ford Motors in India
questions.question: In 1995, American automobile giant Ford Motors entered the Indian market through a joint venture with Mahindra & Mahindra. What mutual benefit did this joint venture deliver?
options: Ford brought global manufacturing technology and capital, while Mahindra provided established domestic component sourcing, dealership networks, and market knowledge
Ford took over the entire railway network of the Indian government
Mahindra was forced to cease all manufacturing operations in India
Ford produced cars exclusively for donation to rural hospitals
questions.explanation: Joint ventures combine local company assets (distribution networks, component vendors, local market understanding) with MNC capital and advanced production technology.

questions.subtopic: Labour Law Flexibility and Insecurity
questions.question: To attract foreign MNC investments, governments in India have permitted 'flexibility in labour laws'. How has this directly affected factory workers?
options: Workers are increasingly hired on short-term contractual basis during peak seasons without job security, paid sick leave, or provident fund benefits
Workers receive permanent lifetime employment contracts with double wages
Workers are appointed as permanent members of company boards of directors
Workers are legally exempt from working more than four hours a week
questions.explanation: In recent years, the government has allowed companies to ignore many labour laws to reduce costs. Instead of hiring workers on a regular basis, companies hire workers 'flexibly' for short periods when there is intense pressure of work, eroding job security.

questions.subtopic: Information Technology Enabling Global Services
questions.question: A news magazine published in London is designed and typeset by software designers in Delhi using telecommunications, printed in Delhi, and flown to London for morning delivery. Which technological forces enable this integrated workflow?
options: High-speed satellite internet, electronic mail, computer desktop publishing, and rapid air cargo transportation
Submarine telegraph cables operating on Morse code
Postal pigeon couriers across the Arabian Sea
Shortwave radio voice broadcasts recorded on magnetic tape
questions.explanation: Information and communication technology (ICT) and air transport have made it possible for service production (design, editing, printing) to be outsourced across continents almost instantaneously.

questions.subtopic: Consumers Benefiting from Globalisation
questions.question: Which socio-economic group in India has gained the most visible and immediate advantages from globalisation?
options: Well-off urban consumers who enjoy a wide variety of high-quality goods (automobiles, cell phones, electronics) at lower competitive prices
Landless rural agricultural sharecroppers
Small cottage plastic and capacitor producers
Unskilled contract garment stitching workers
questions.explanation: Globalisation and greater competition among producers has been of greatest advantage to urban consumers. There is greater choice before these consumers who now enjoy improved quality and lower prices for several products.

questions.subtopic: Small Industries Vulnerability in India
questions.question: Which manufacturing sectors in India were severely hit by cheap foreign imports following the removal of trade barriers under WTO rules?
options: Batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products, and vegetable oil
Heavy commercial railway coaches and locomotives
Nuclear energy reactors and rocket launch vehicles
Handwritten royal parchment manuscripts
questions.explanation: Batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products, and vegetable vegetable oil are examples of industries where small manufacturers have been hit hard due to competition. Several units have shut down, leaving workers jobless.

questions.subtopic: Garment Export Industry and Sweatshop Conditions
questions.question: In the NCERT case of garment worker Sushila in an export factory in Delhi, why did her conditions deteriorate from 2000 onwards?
options: To meet tight deadlines and rock-bottom prices demanded by foreign MNC brands, the factory laid off permanent staff and made workers like Sushila temporary daily-wagers working 12-hour shifts without benefits
The factory was nationalized by the central government and converted into a hospital
Sushila was promoted to chief executive officer of a European retail chain
The factory relocated all sewing machines to international waters
questions.explanation: To get orders from MNCs, garment exporters cut costs ruthlessly. Since raw material costs cannot be reduced, they cut labour costs by hiring temporary workers for long hours (12+ hours) without overtime or social security.
questions.citation: NCERT Class 10 Economics, Chapter 4, Section 4.4 (Case of Sushila)

questions.subtopic: Government Policies for Fair Globalisation
questions.question: How can the government ensure that the benefits of globalisation are shared equitably across all citizens?
options: By properly implementing labour laws to protect worker rights, supporting small producers until they become competitive, and judiciously using trade barriers when necessary
By shutting down all international airports and seaports
By abolishing corporate taxes completely for all foreign companies
By banning Indian students from studying computer engineering abroad
questions.explanation: The government can ensure that labour laws are properly implemented and the workers get their rights. It can support small producers to improve their performance until they become strong enough to compete. If necessary, the government can use trade and investment barriers.

questions.subtopic: Civil Society and People's Campaigns against WTO
questions.question: In recent decades, massive protests and public campaigns organized by civil society groups and developing nations have successfully demonstrated that:
options: People's collective political mobilization can influence critical decisions related to international trade and investment rules at the WTO
The WTO only accepts advice from private multinational CEOs
Public demonstrations are legally banned under international treaties
Developing nations have zero voting voice in global forums
questions.explanation: Massive campaigns and representation by people's organisations have influenced important decisions relating to trade and investments at the WTO. This has demonstrated that people also can play an important role in the struggle for fair globalisation.

questions.subtopic: Top Indian Companies Benefiting from Foreign Technology
questions.question: How have leading Indian firms (such as automobile parts manufacturers) prospered from the entry of foreign MNCs into India?
options: They upgraded their production technology, invested in newer machinery, raised quality standards, and became global suppliers to multinational corporations
They ceased all production and leased their factories to foreign armies
They were banned from selling auto parts to Indian consumers
They replaced all electrical machines with manual hand tools
questions.explanation: Several top Indian companies have been able to benefit from the increased competition. They have invested in newer technology and production methods and raised their production standards. Some have gained from successful collaborations with foreign companies.

questions.subtopic: BPO and IT Outsourcing to India
questions.question: Why has India emerged as the world's leading destination for Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) and software IT services?
options: A large pool of skilled English-speaking technical graduates working at significantly lower wages than in Western developed nations
The Indian government pays the salaries of all foreign software engineers
India has banned all domestic manufacturing industries
Computers in India operate twice as fast as in other continents
questions.explanation: India combines a large demographic of educated, English-fluent engineers and science graduates with low relative labour costs and reliable digital connectivity, making it a global IT outsourcing hub.

questions.subtopic: Developing Nations Alliance at WTO
questions.question: At WTO ministerial conferences, why do developing countries (like India, South Africa, and Brazil) frequently form negotiation coalitions?
options: To pool their collective bargaining power and challenge the unfair trade dominance and agricultural subsidies maintained by rich developed nations
To declare military war against developed economies
To ban all foreign container ships from docking at their ports
To force the WTO to relocate its headquarters to Antarctica
questions.explanation: Developing countries align together at the WTO to resist pressure from rich nations, demanding the elimination of rich-country agricultural subsidies and safeguarding food security.

questions.subtopic: MNC Leverage over Small Suppliers
questions.question: How do giant global retail brands (such as Nike, Walmart, and Gap) exercise enormous economic leverage over small apparel factories in developing countries?
options: They dictate price, quality specifications, delivery deadlines, and labour conditions because suppliers compete fiercely among themselves for limited purchase contracts
They own 100% of the land in developing country export zones
They are legally authorized to arrest small factory managers who make sewing errors
They pay suppliers five years in advance without inspecting goods
questions.explanation: The MNCs have tremendous power to determine price, quality, delivery, and labour conditions for these distant producers because suppliers have little bargaining power and face intense competition.

questions.subtopic: Foreign Direct Investment vs Foreign Portfolio Investment
questions.question: What is the key difference between Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) and Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI)?
options: FDI involves long-term physical capital investment in factories and operations with management control, whereas FPI involves purchasing stocks and bonds on domestic financial markets without direct control
FDI is strictly illegal under Indian law, while FPI is fully permitted
FDI is carried out exclusively in gold bullion, while FPI uses currency notes
FDI only applies to agricultural farms, while FPI applies to space exploration
questions.explanation: FDI establishes tangible physical assets (plants, joint ventures) with long-term strategic control, whereas FPI is financial capital investing in traded securities.

questions.subtopic: Impact of Tariff Removal on Small Farmers
questions.question: If India were to eliminate all import tariffs on agricultural products like wheat, dairy, and cotton, what would happen to small Indian farmers?
options: They would face severe price crashes and bankruptcy due to subsidized foreign agricultural surpluses dumped on Indian markets
They would immediately become the wealthiest farmers on Earth
Their crop yields would automatically double within two weeks
They would be hired as senior corporate executives by foreign agribusinesses
questions.explanation: Unrestricted imports of heavily subsidized Western crops would flood domestic mandis at below-cost prices, destroying the livelihoods of millions of small subsistence farmers.

questions.subtopic: Technology as Catalyst for Market Integration
questions.question: Which of the following technological innovations has contributed most decisively to integrating financial markets across the globe in real time?
options: High-speed fiber-optic telecommunications and global electronic fund transfer networks
Coal-powered steamships and postal mail packets
Typewriters and carbon-copy printing presses
Mechanical pocket watches and abacuses
questions.explanation: Internet, satellite links, and electronic fund transfers allow billions of dollars in trade and investment to move across continents in milliseconds, integrating global capital markets.

questions.subtopic: Special Economic Zones: Land Acquisition Controversy
questions.question: Why has the creation of Special Economic Zones (SEZs) in India sometimes faced severe domestic resistance and protests?
options: Because fertile multi-crop agricultural land was acquired from farmers, displacing rural families and depriving agricultural labourers of livelihoods
Because SEZs refuse to produce manufactured goods
Because foreign MNCs are barred from entering SEZ zones
Because SEZs do not have electricity or road connections
questions.explanation: Setting up SEZs has often involved acquiring fertile farmland, causing loss of agricultural livelihoods and displacement of local communities without adequate rehabilitation.

questions.subtopic: Consumer Culture and Globalisation
questions.question: How has globalisation transformed the consumer retail landscape in Indian metropolitan cities over the last twenty years?
options: Shoppers now have immediate access to the latest global brands in smartphones, cars, designer clothing, and international food chains
All retail shopping malls have been replaced by traditional barter mandis
Foreign electronic goods are completely banned from store shelves
Consumers are restricted to buying only locally produced khadi cotton
questions.explanation: Consumers in India today have a wide variety of goods and services before them. The latest models of digital cameras, mobile phones and television sets made by leading manufacturers of the world are within their reach.

questions.subtopic: Flexibility of Capital vs Immobility of Labour
questions.question: What fundamental asymmetry exists between capital and labour in the contemporary globalised economy?
options: Capital and MNC investments can move across borders with tremendous freedom and speed, while human labour faces strict visa restrictions and immigration controls
Human workers can move freely across all borders without passports, while capital is legally locked in home nations
Neither capital nor labour is permitted to cross national borders
Multinational corporations are legally prohibited from transferring profits to home countries
questions.explanation: While globalisation has drastically accelerated the movement of goods, capital, and technology across borders, international movement of labour remains severely restricted by national immigration barriers.

questions.subtopic: Role of Judiciary in Protecting Labour Rights
questions.question: When export-oriented factories ignore statutory safety rules and fire workers arbitrarily to lower production costs, what institutional remedy is available in a constitutional democracy?
options: Workers and labour unions can approach labour tribunals and High Courts to enforce statutory rights under the Industrial Disputes Act and Factories Act
Workers must surrender their citizenship and leave the country
Judicial courts are legally prohibited from hearing cases involving foreign MNCs
Workers must seek authorization from the World Trade Organisation
questions.explanation: Democratic judicial institutions (labour courts, High Courts, Supreme Court) possess constitutional authority to strike down arbitrary dismissals and enforce labour welfare protections.

questions.subtopic: Summary: Balanced Globalisation
questions.question: Which of the following encapsulates the consensus view of economists on the impact of globalisation in India?
options: Globalisation has brought immense technological modernization and consumer choice, but has generated uneven outcomes, benefiting corporate elites while intensifying insecurity for small producers and informal workers
Globalisation has had 100% negative effects with zero benefits for any Indian citizen
Globalisation has completely eliminated all poverty and unemployment across rural India
Globalisation has had no measurable effect on Indian trade or lifestyle
questions.explanation: Globalisation has been a mixed blessing: it stimulated growth, tech modernization, and consumer welfare, but created precarious contract labour and severely challenged small unorganized producers.
questions.citation: NCERT Class 10 Economics, Chapter 4, Chapter Overview
